intro: The Danish String Quartet plays the C minor Adagio from Haydn’s Quartet in C major, Op. 54 No. 2, in which the first violin plays lines in the manner of an improvisation above a hymn in the other three instruments. Haydn left the ending open and runs the movement straight into the minuet.

sections.label: A · C minor, violin over chorale
sections.mNote: The first violin decorates the slow melody of the lower three.

sections.label: B · Changing chords beneath the violin
sections.mNote: The violin moves above the held accompaniment.

sections.label: C · C minor, then a held G
sections.mNote: Morendo; the music dies away before the minuet.

cues.title: Chorale with first violin, C minor
cues.text: The second violin, viola and cello play a slow melody in C minor. Above them the first violin plays quick, elaborate flourishes.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Adagio, pp. 188–190. Laurie Shulman describes the first violin’s rhapsodic line above a chorale in the other three instruments: https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First violin over chorale accompaniment
cues.text: The lower instruments hold their notes while the first violin plays an ornamental line above them. Its turns and leaps run across the chords. The accompaniment keeps a steady pace.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Adagio, pp. 188–189; Shulman’s account of the ornamental violin line and chorale accompaniment. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Johann Tost in Paris, 1788
cues.text: In late 1788 Johann Tost travelled to Paris with six new Haydn quartets and two symphonies. Until March of that year he had been principal second violin in the Esterházy orchestra. In Paris he did business with the publisher Sieber.
cues.evidence: Laurie Shulman, programme note for the Schumann Quartet, 20 November 2022, p. 2: Tost’s service, Paris visit and negotiations. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf

cues.title: Rosemary Hughes on Op. 54 No. 2
cues.text: Haydn’s biographer Rosemary Hughes described the first violin breaking into “impassioned arabesques above the dark and brooding melody, in the manner of a wild Hungarian lament”. The first violin has an unusually prominent role in all twelve of the Tost quartets, Opp. 54, 55 and 64.
cues.evidence: Rosemary Hughes on Op. 54 No. 2, quoted in Laurie Shulman’s programme note for the Schumann Quartet, 20 November 2022, p. 2. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf

cues.title: Ending and attacca to the minuet
cues.text: The closing passage is marked morendo, dying away. The movement ends on a held G in C minor, under a fermata. Haydn marks it attacca, and the C major minuet follows without a break.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, p. 190: morendo, final G with fermata and attacca. Shulman confirms the unbroken connection to the Menuetto. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

timeline.note: The first violin decorates the slow melody shared by the other three players.
The first violin keeps moving above the sustained chords of the lower instruments.
Marked morendo, the quartet fades towards a held G, then continues into the minuet.

composer.epithet: Composer known for an orchestral work in which the players leave one at a time, and for a quartet that continues after listeners think it has ended.

quote.text: The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I.
quote.source: London notebook, after his benefit concert on 4 May 1795; our translation

composer.background:
On 4 May 1795, Haydn gave a benefit concert at the King’s Theatre in London. The programme included his new D major Symphony, now numbered 104. Afterwards he wrote in his notebook: “The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I. I made four thousand gulden this evening. Such a thing can only be done in England.” He was sixty-three. He was a wheelwright’s son and had spent most of his adult life in the livery of a servant of the Esterházy family.

Haydn was born in Rohrau in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who played the harp by ear and sang; his mother had worked as a cook. At about six, Joseph left home for schooling in Hainburg. By 1740 he was a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. As a chorister he sang church music daily but received little instruction in composition. Performances outside the cathedral also gave him chances to get a meal. When his voice broke and he was dismissed in 1749, another musician, Johann Michael Spangler, took him into his family’s crowded room.
